meta.source: Virginia DWR / MD DNR / NPS waterbody species documentation
meta.note: Documented species per waterbody; attached to matching access points as shared-waterbody official listings (not access-point angler reports).
meta.byWaterbodyNote: Per-named-water DWR fish communities (waterbody pages + fisheries reports).

tidal-potomac.summary: Virginia DWR reports excellent largemouth bass fishing in the tidal Potomac, with 2025 adult catch rates the highest documented in 21 years of standardized surveys.
tidal-potomac.strengthNote: Adult bass electrofishing catch rates the highest since standardized surveys began 21 years ago; a premier East Coast largemouth fishery.

tidal-potomac.summary: Virginia DWR documents an established northern snakehead fishery in the tidal Potomac and its northern creeks, rated average-to-below-average for 2026.
tidal-potomac.strengthNote: Snakehead fishing expected average in Aquia Creek, below average in many other northern Potomac creeks below DC.

tidal-potomac.summary: Virginia DWR documents blue catfish (an established invasive) as a targetable species across its tidal rivers including the Potomac, where trophy fish are common.
tidal-potomac.strengthNote: Trophy-caliber blue catfish common in tidal Potomac backwaters and tributaries; DWR notes excellent catfishing across Virginia tidal rivers.

tidal-potomac.summary: Virginia DWR lists striped bass among the migratory species of the tidal Potomac River.
Virginia DWR documents white perch as a species anglers can target on its tidal rivers including the Potomac.
Virginia DWR documents yellow perch among the species targetable on its tidal rivers including the Potomac.
Virginia DWR lists carp among the top targetable species of the tidal Potomac River.
Channel catfish are documented as a resident catfish species of Virginia's tidal rivers including the tidal Potomac.

nontidal-potomac.summary: Maryland DNR calls smallmouth bass the most sought-after gamefish in the nontidal Potomac River, with quality- and preferred-size populations above established benchmarks.
nontidal-potomac.strengthNote: Quality-size (11"+) and preferred-size (14"+) fish have increased above benchmarks; supplemental stocking 2019-2024 buffered high-flow year-classes.

nontidal-potomac.summary: Maryland DNR documents walleye throughout the nontidal Potomac, with the highest densities from Dam 5 downstream to Point of Rocks.
nontidal-potomac.strengthNote: Roughly 37-40% of the population exceeds 15 inches; managed under a 15-20" slot with a January-April harvest window.

nontidal-potomac.summary: Maryland DNR describes muskellunge as an exciting, relatively new addition to the Potomac River sport fishery supported by a dedicated Maryland Muskie Program.
nontidal-potomac.strengthNote: Established via a managed muskie program on the upper river.

nontidal-potomac.summary: Maryland DNR reports a relatively stable channel catfish population in the nontidal Potomac.
nontidal-potomac.strengthNote: Electrofishing surveys show ~40-60 channel catfish per hour, roughly three-quarters in the 12-20 inch range.

nontidal-potomac.summary: Maryland DNR lists largemouth bass among the gamefish managed in the nontidal Potomac River.
Maryland DNR documents invasive flathead catfish in the nontidal Potomac and encourages anglers to harvest all they catch.
nontidal-potomac.strengthNote: Apex predator with a documented threefold abundance increase from 2016 to 2021; targeted for removal.

nontidal-potomac.summary: The National Park Service documents invasive northern snakehead as established in the Potomac River along the C&O Canal / Great Falls corridor.
nontidal-potomac.strengthNote: Invasive; NPS instructs anglers not to release and to report catches.

occoquan-reservoir.summary: Virginia DWR ranks Occoquan Reservoir's largemouth bass fishery as the best in the district for CPUE of preferred fish over 15 inches.
occoquan-reservoir.strengthNote: Best in district for CPUE of 15in+ fish; good numbers in the 4-6 lb range, fish up to 21 in.

occoquan-reservoir.summary: Virginia DWR documents a balanced bluegill population in Occoquan Reservoir.
occoquan-reservoir.strengthNote: Fair numbers in the 5-7 inch range; population declined since the early 1990s but remains balanced.

occoquan-reservoir.summary: Virginia DWR documents black crappie as part of Occoquan Reservoir's very good crappie fishery.
occoquan-reservoir.strengthNote: Reservoir has a very good crappie fishery; fish structure in early spring.

occoquan-reservoir.summary: Virginia DWR notes Occoquan is the only District lake to offer white crappie, which typically run larger.
occoquan-reservoir.strengthNote: Only District lake with white crappie; white crappie typically run larger than black.

occoquan-reservoir.summary: Virginia DWR documents a self-sustaining channel catfish population in Occoquan Reservoir.
occoquan-reservoir.strengthNote: Self-sustaining; fish typically 14-20 inches averaging about 2 pounds.

occoquan-reservoir.summary: Virginia DWR documents flathead catfish in Occoquan Reservoir, which produced a former state record.
occoquan-reservoir.strengthNote: Produced the previous state record flathead catfish of 66 lb 4 oz (May 1994).

occoquan-reservoir.summary: Virginia DWR lists white perch as a managed species present in Occoquan Reservoir.
Virginia DWR's 2022 fisheries management report documents yellow perch among Occoquan Reservoir's supported populations.

pohick-belmont-bay.summary: Virginia DWR forecasts excellent largemouth bass fishing in the tidal Potomac including Pohick Creek, with 2025 electrofishing catch rates the highest in 21 years.
pohick-belmont-bay.strengthNote: Pohick Creek adult bass catch rates routinely over 100/hour; regional catch rates the best since standardized surveys began.

pohick-belmont-bay.summary: Virginia DWR documents northern snakehead throughout the tidal Potomac tributaries including Pohick Creek, though numbers have stabilized below historical peaks.
pohick-belmont-bay.strengthNote: Established but at reduced/average levels in northern tributaries versus earlier highs.

pohick-belmont-bay.summary: Virginia DWR lists white perch in the tidal Occoquan River / Belmont Bay.
Virginia DWR lists striped bass in the tidal Occoquan River / Belmont Bay.
Virginia DWR lists yellow perch in the tidal Occoquan River / Belmont Bay.
Virginia DWR lists channel catfish in the tidal Occoquan River / Belmont Bay.
Virginia DWR lists flathead catfish in the tidal Occoquan River / Belmont Bay.
Virginia DWR lists crappie in the tidal Occoquan River / Belmont Bay (species not specified; black crappie is the predominant tidal Potomac crappie).
pohick-belmont-bay.strengthNote: DWR names only 'crappie'; mapped to black crappie as the dominant tidal-Potomac species.

beaverdam-reservoir.summary: Virginia DWR documents largemouth bass as the reservoir's premier fishery, with excellent condition and desirable size structure recovering after the drawdown.
beaverdam-reservoir.strengthNote: 2022 CPUE 55/hr, PSD 88, two memorable 20-inch bass; condition rated excellent from abundant forage.

beaverdam-reservoir.summary: Virginia DWR documents bluegill as present with a moderate catch rate but poor size structure in Beaverdam Creek Reservoir.
beaverdam-reservoir.strengthNote: 2022 CPUE 65/hr but all fish under 8 inches; size structure limited by competition from white perch and gizzard shad.

beaverdam-reservoir.summary: Virginia DWR lists black crappie in the current fishery, though limited numbers remain after the extended drawdown.
beaverdam-reservoir.strengthNote: No crappie collected in 2022; 2020 sample produced twelve fish around 5 inches; population likely limited post-drawdown.

beaverdam-reservoir.summary: Virginia DWR includes common carp in the current fishery of Beaverdam Creek Reservoir.
Virginia DWR reports white perch as one of the most abundant species in Beaverdam Creek Reservoir.
beaverdam-reservoir.strengthNote: Found up to 7 inches; prone to overpopulating and stunting, so anglers encouraged to harvest this abundant resource.

beaverdam-reservoir.summary: Virginia DWR lists channel catfish in the current fishery of Beaverdam Creek Reservoir, originally stocked in 1973.
beaverdam-reservoir.strengthNote: Regulations allow 8 per day with a 15-inch minimum.

lake-anna-region-check.summary: Virginia DWR documents muskellunge in the Main Stem Shenandoah River (Warren County, NOVA region), sustained by annual fingerling stocking from Warren Dam to Route 7 landing.
lake-anna-region-check.strengthNote: Adult musky densities described as low but resembling a wild reproducing population; best water is directly below Warren Dam. South Fork densities noted as excellent where deep pool habitat exists.

lake-anna-region-check.summary: Virginia DWR documents white crappie in the Main Stem Shenandoah River (NOVA region), present but subordinate to black crappie.
lake-anna-region-check.strengthNote: Crappie densities are low; encountered in fair numbers mainly in deep pools, with black crappie the more dominant of the two species.

Lake Brittle.summary: Virginia DWR documents largemouth bass as the primary sport fish and a very good fishery at Lake Brittle.
Lake Brittle.strengthNote: Very good fishery; fish average 2-3 pounds.

Lake Brittle.summary: Virginia DWR documents bluegill as abundant in Lake Brittle, though the population is stunted.
Lake Brittle.strengthNote: Abundant but stunted; poor size structure.

Lake Brittle.summary: Virginia DWR documents black crappie in Lake Brittle as a stunted fishery with poor growth rates.
Virginia DWR confirms an existing channel catfish population remains in Lake Brittle, but stocking is discontinued until further notice and catch rates may decline over time.
Lake Brittle.strengthNote: Existing population remains; stocking discontinued; DWR warns catch rates may decline.

Lake Brittle.summary: Virginia DWR has stocked walleye in Lake Brittle since 1979 as a put-and-grow fishery.
Virginia DWR documents flathead catfish as self-sustaining in Lake Brittle after 1990s stockings.
Lake Brittle.strengthNote: Self-sustaining since 1990/1994 stockings; introduced as a predator.

Lake Brittle.summary: Virginia DWR documents northern snakehead in Lake Brittle as established and apparently self-sustaining since 2015.

Lake Curtis.summary: Virginia DWR documents Lake Curtis as an excellent, trophy-class largemouth bass fishery.
Lake Curtis.strengthNote: Excellent; produces large bass, with fish as heavy as 13 pounds; 15-inch minimum.

Lake Curtis.summary: Virginia DWR describes Lake Curtis as offering the finest bluegill fishery in the district.
Lake Curtis.strengthNote: Finest bluegill fishery in the district.

Lake Curtis.summary: Virginia DWR documents an excellent channel catfish population in Lake Curtis.

Rocky Pen Run Reservoir.summary: Virginia DWR documents largemouth bass as an abundant, naturally colonized fishery in this Stafford reservoir (now cataloged as Lake Mooney).
Rocky Pen Run Reservoir.strengthNote: Abundant, high catch rates; fish over 18 inches sampled and anglers report bass over 10 pounds.

Rocky Pen Run Reservoir.summary: Virginia DWR documents black crappie as naturally colonized and abundant, though stockpiling at smaller sizes, in this reservoir (Lake Mooney).
Rocky Pen Run Reservoir.strengthNote: Abundant but small; harvest to statewide creel limit encouraged.

Rocky Pen Run Reservoir.summary: Virginia DWR stocked bluegill into this reservoir (Lake Mooney) during its 2014-2016 fill.
Virginia DWR stocked channel catfish into this reservoir (Lake Mooney) during its 2014-2016 fill.

Silver Lake.summary: Virginia DWR lists largemouth bass among the catchable species at Silver Lake Regional Park.
Virginia DWR lists channel catfish at Silver Lake, noting stocking has been discontinued so catch rates may decline.
Virginia DWR lists bluegill sunfish among the catchable species at Silver Lake.
Virginia DWR lists black crappie among the catchable species at Silver Lake.

Locust Shade Pond.summary: Virginia DWR documents channel catfish as stocked each spring at Locust Shade Park pond (stockings currently discontinued until further notice).
Virginia DWR documents Locust Shade Park as an urban trout stocking site with five stockings from November 1 through April 30 (stocked catchable trout).
Virginia DWR documents a resident largemouth bass population at Locust Shade Park pond.
Virginia DWR documents a resident bluegill population at Locust Shade Park pond.

Lake Shenandoah.summary: Virginia DWR describes the Lake Shenandoah largemouth bass fishery as fair with a good size distribution.
Lake Shenandoah.strengthNote: Fair; fish 9-15 in make up the bulk

Lake Shenandoah.summary: Virginia DWR documents black crappie at Lake Shenandoah, historically stunted but with improving sizes.
Virginia DWR documents abundant bluegill at Lake Shenandoah with good numbers and high catch rates though moderately stunted.
Lake Shenandoah.strengthNote: Good numbers, high catch rates; few over 6 in

Lake Shenandoah.summary: Virginia DWR documents channel catfish at Lake Shenandoah with modest catch rates of 12-20 inch fish; stocking discontinued.
Virginia DWR lists common carp among the species anglers can catch at Lake Shenandoah.
Virginia DWR calls muskellunge the bright spot at Lake Shenandoah, stocked annually and offering a great opportunity to catch a trophy species.

Mountain Run Lake.summary: Virginia DWR describes largemouth bass as providing good fishing at Mountain Run Lake.
Virginia DWR's 2023 fisheries report documents an exact-water Black Crappie fishery at Mountain Run Reservoir, including April 2022 electrofishing results.
Mountain Run Lake.strengthNote: Adequate fishery; exact species documented in the 2022 sample.

Mountain Run Lake.summary: Virginia DWR lists bluegill among the species at Mountain Run Lake.
Virginia DWR describes the Mountain Run Lake channel catfish population as among the best found in a small impoundment in Northern Virginia.
Mountain Run Lake.strengthNote: Among the best small-impoundment catfish in NoVa

Lake Orange.summary: Virginia DWR describes largemouth bass fishing at Lake Orange as very good, with numerous 10-12 inch fish and a decent number of 15-18 inch fish.
Lake Orange.strengthNote: Very good; 10-12 in numerous, some 15-18 in

Lake Orange.summary: Virginia DWR describes the Lake Orange black crappie population as healthy and abundant and in good condition.
Virginia DWR documents a decent walleye fishery at Lake Orange, stocked regularly with 4-5 pound fish caught routinely.
Virginia DWR documents a good channel catfish fishery at Lake Orange with numerous fish in the 2-pound-plus range (stockings discontinued until further notice).
Virginia DWR documents abundant bluegill at Lake Orange averaging 6-7 inches.
Virginia DWR lists yellow perch among the species present at Lake Orange.
Virginia DWR lists white perch among the species present at Lake Orange.
Virginia DWR lists common carp among the species present at Lake Orange.

Lake Frederick.summary: Virginia DWR documents largemouth bass as an excellent, high-quality fishery in Lake Frederick, historically the best in the Shenandoah Valley.
Lake Frederick.strengthNote: Excellent population; many 2-4 lb fish, some up to 10 lb

Lake Frederick.summary: Virginia DWR documents bluegill/sunfish as producing good numbers of large, hand-sized fish in Lake Frederick.
Lake Frederick.strengthNote: Only regional lake producing good numbers of large sunfish; hand-sized

Lake Frederick.summary: Virginia DWR documents black crappie as a healthy population in Lake Frederick with fish of harvestable size.
Virginia DWR documents channel catfish in fantastic numbers in Lake Frederick, historically stocked annually.
Lake Frederick.strengthNote: Fantastic numbers; fish over 25 inches; stocking discontinued

Lake Fairfax.summary: Virginia DWR documents bluegill as present in Lake Fairfax.
Virginia DWR documents largemouth bass as present in Lake Fairfax.
Virginia DWR documents channel catfish in Lake Fairfax, though stocking has been discontinued.
Lake Fairfax.strengthNote: Stocking discontinued; expect lower catch rates over time

Lake Fairfax.summary: Virginia DWR documents crappie as present in Lake Fairfax.

Lake Burke.summary: Virginia DWR documents the largemouth bass population of Burke Lake as in excellent condition.
Lake Burke.strengthNote: Excellent; averaging ~3 lb, 6 lb fish common

Lake Burke.summary: Virginia DWR documents Burke Lake as a stocked trophy muskellunge fishery.
Lake Burke.strengthNote: Trophy fishery; numerous 20-25 lb fish; 49.25 inch fish netted

Lake Burke.summary: Virginia DWR documents walleye in Burke Lake and describes annual stocking on the current waterbody page.
Lake Burke.strengthNote: Stocked 100/acre; anglers catch 4-7 lb fish, some over 9 lb

Lake Burke.summary: Virginia DWR documents a good channel catfish fishery in Burke Lake.
Lake Burke.strengthNote: Numerous 10-15 lb fish; lake record 21 lb 8 oz; stocking discontinued

Lake Burke.summary: Virginia DWR documents an abundant bluegill population in Burke Lake.
Virginia DWR documents a decent black crappie fishery in Burke Lake.
Lake Burke.strengthNote: Numerous 6-8 inch fish; lake record 3.5 lb

Lake Burke.summary: Virginia DWR documents white perch as present in Burke Lake.
Virginia DWR documents yellow perch as present in Burke Lake.
Virginia DWR documents occasional blue catfish in Burke Lake.
Virginia DWR documents northern snakehead as an established invasive target in Burke Lake.
Lake Burke.strengthNote: Invasive; popular fly and spin target

Beaverdam Reservoir.summary: Virginia DWR lists largemouth bass as the best bet in Beaverdam Creek Reservoir.
Beaverdam Reservoir.strengthNote: Best bet; ranks 11th of 18 district impoundments for preferred bass catch

Beaverdam Reservoir.summary: Virginia DWR documents bluegill, maintained by natural reproduction, in Beaverdam Creek Reservoir.
Virginia DWR documents black crappie as a popular fishery in Beaverdam Creek Reservoir.
Virginia DWR documents common carp as present in Beaverdam Creek Reservoir.
Virginia DWR documents white perch as present in Beaverdam Creek Reservoir.
Virginia DWR documents channel catfish as present in Beaverdam Creek Reservoir.

Occoquan River.summary: Virginia DWR documents white perch in the tidal Occoquan River.
Virginia DWR documents striped bass in the tidal Occoquan River.
Virginia DWR documents largemouth bass in the tidal Occoquan River.
Virginia DWR documents crappie in the tidal Occoquan River.
Occoquan River.strengthNote: DWR page lists generic 'crappie'; mapped to black crappie, the dominant tidal-freshwater crappie

Occoquan River.summary: Virginia DWR documents yellow perch in the tidal Occoquan River.
Virginia DWR documents flathead catfish in the tidal Occoquan River.
Virginia DWR documents channel catfish in the tidal Occoquan River.

Accotink Creek.summary: Virginia DWR designates Accotink Creek (Fairfax County) a delayed-harvest stocked trout water, where rainbow trout are the primary stocked species.
Accotink Creek.strengthNote: Delayed-harvest fishery: Oct 1-May 31 catch-and-release, artificial lures only; stocked put-and-take otherwise.

Holmes Run.summary: Virginia DWR designates Holmes Run (Fairfax County) a delayed-harvest stocked trout water, where rainbow trout are the primary stocked species.
Holmes Run.strengthNote: Delayed-harvest fishery: Oct 1-May 31 catch-and-release, artificial lures only; stocked put-and-take otherwise.

Quantico Creek.summary: The NPS Prince William Forest Park fishing page documents largemouth bass as one of the most commonly found fish in Quantico Creek.
Quantico Creek.strengthNote: Listed among the most commonly caught species

Quantico Creek.summary: The NPS Prince William Forest Park fishing page documents channel catfish among the most commonly found fish in Quantico Creek.
Quantico Creek.strengthNote: Listed among the most commonly caught species

Quantico Creek.summary: The NPS Prince William Forest Park fishing page documents bluegill among the most commonly found fish in Quantico Creek.
Quantico Creek.strengthNote: Listed among the most commonly caught species

Quantico Creek.summary: The NPS Prince William Forest Park fishing page notes northern snakehead as a documented invasive species present in the park's waters including Quantico Creek.

Neabsco Creek.summary: Virginia DWR documents northern snakehead as very abundant throughout the tidal Potomac tributaries, which include Neabsco Creek.
Neabsco Creek.strengthNote: Described as very abundant in tidal Potomac tributaries

Hazel River.summary: Virginia DWR (Upper Rappahannock waterbody page) describes the Hazel River as a good smallmouth stream in its own right.
Hazel River.strengthNote: Described as a good smallmouth stream

North Fork Thornton River.summary: Virginia DWR's North Fork Thornton River waterbody page documents an excellent native brook trout population within Shenandoah National Park near Sperryville.

Robinson River.summary: Virginia DWR lists the Robinson River (Madison County) as a Category A designated stocked trout water stocked with rainbow trout eight times per season plus a Heritage Day stocking.
Robinson River.strengthNote: Primary catchable stocked species; Category A water stocked 8x/season plus Heritage Day event.

Robinson River.summary: Virginia DWR documents brook trout among the trout stocked in the Robinson River, Madison County.
Robinson River.strengthNote: Secondary stocked species alongside rainbow trout.

Rose River.summary: Virginia DWR lists the Rose River (Madison County) as a Category A designated stocked trout water stocked eight times between October and May, primarily with rainbow trout.
Rose River.strengthNote: Primary catchable stocked species; Category A water stocked 8x/season.
